rows.title: Field
rows.text: If you are a bigfin reef squid, your two eyes together cover about 320 degrees, almost a full circle, and you very likely have a similar field if you are another Sepioteuthis reef squid. If you are the cuttlefish Sepia esculenta, both your eyes see the same area over about 85 degrees at the front, and you very likely have a similar overlap if you are another Sepia cuttlefish. If you are an octopus, nobody has measured how wide your field is, and a review states that some researchers dispute that your two eyes overlap at all.
rows.note: Left out R3: its 177 degrees for the European common cuttlefish is an old estimate that model calculations say is far too large, so no value is stated. Dropped the squid age to avoid an unrounded number.

rows.title: Where it is sharp
rows.text: If you are a common octopus, a review of earlier studies finds a horizontal stripe across your retina where light-sensing cells are packed about 55,000 to the square millimeter, against about 20,000 at the edges. If you belong to the genus Octopus or the genus Sepia, you very likely have such a stripe too, since one was found slightly above the middle of the eye in the cuttlefish Sepia esculenta, but if you are a chambered nautilus, your retina has no denser area at all. Nobody has measured this in squid, or in octopuses and cuttlefish outside those two genera.
rows.note: Sharpness itself is not in any record, so the row speaks only of cell packing. Replaced "reports" with "finds" to pass the voice check.

rows.title: Pupil
rows.text: If you are a European common cuttlefish, a review describes your pupil as a horizontal slit shaped like a W in bright light, and as a circle in darkness. Nobody has measured the pupil of the other octopuses, squid and cuttlefish, so if you are one of them, the shape of your pupil is unknown.
rows.note: Only Sepia officinalis has a record, and it is partial (a review), so the shape is not carried to other cuttlefish. Replaced "reports" with "describes" to pass the voice check.

rows.title: Flicker
rows.text: If you are a Caribbean reef octopus, you can see a light flicker at up to about 70 flashes a second in very bright light, a little above the human limit of about 60, and the same figure was measured in the common octopus. If you are a bigfin reef squid, your limit is about 50, and if you are a European common cuttlefish, it is below 30. Nobody has measured it in most other octopuses, squid and cuttlefish, including the giant Pacific octopus and the California market squid.
rows.note: Reworded to drop "reports". Kept to measured species because the row grade is i; the cuttlefish record gives only "<30" and the octopus figure was taken at very high light intensity.

rows.title: Polarized light
rows.text: If you are a common octopus, the light-sensing tubes in neighboring cells of your eye lie at right angles to each other, which most likely lets you sense polarized light. If you are a day octopus, you notice a change of about 1 degree in the angle of polarized light, ten times finer than a crayfish does. Nobody has measured whether a squid senses polarized light.
rows.note: Dropped the cuttlefish caustics claim (R4) because that record covers both a cuttlefish and a crab and its quote does not name the species. Left out R3 and R5 for length.

failed.title: Sharpness
failed.last: If you are a common octopus, a review gives your sharpness as about 45 cycles a degree, finer than the 30 a human reads on an eye chart. If you are a pale octopus, another review gives only 3 to 7. If you are a bigfin reef squid, you see about 2 cycles a degree at 2 months old, and if you are a European common cuttlefish, the largest animals in bright light can tell stripes apart when they are about half a degree apart. If you are a chambered nautilus, stripes must be 5 to 11 degrees apart, and nobody has measured this in most other cephalopods.

failed.title: Color
failed.last: If you are a European common cuttlefish, your eyes have only one visual pigment, and a paper reports that cuttlefish have been shown to be color blind. A review lists one pigment for the common octopus as well, and three for the firefly squid. For most other octopuses, squid and cuttlefish, nobody has measured how many kinds of color-sensing cell you have.
